STAFF REPORT


DATE:       October 21, 2026
To:         TRPA Governing Board
From:       TRPA Staff
Subject:    Briefing on Biodiversity and Recreation Threshold Updates


Summary and Staff Recommendation:
The Bi-State Compact requires TRPA to adopt environmental threshold carrying capacities (threshold
standards) to establish environmental quality goals for the Tahoe Region. The Board identified
continuing to review and update the standards as a priority for the 2026-2027 work plan. The
presentation will provide an overview of the work underway to update threshold standards related to
biodiversity and recreation.

Requested Action:
This item is informational only.
Background:
More than forty years ago, the revised Bi-State Compact recognized that “the waters of Lake Tahoe and
other resources of the region are threatened with deterioration or degeneration, which endangers the
natural beauty and economic productivity of the region” (96th Congress, 1980). To protect these
resources for future generations, the Compact directs TRPA to establish “environmental threshold
carrying capacities,” defined as “an environmental standard necessary to maintain a significant scenic,
recreation, educational, scientific or natural value of the region or to maintain public health and safety
within the region.”
These standards set environmental quality goals and represent a shared aspiration to restore and
protect Lake Tahoe. The standards shape the goals and policies of the Regional Plan and guide millions
of dollars of public and private investment in the basin through the Environmental Improvement
Program (EIP).
The initial threshold standards, established more than four decades ago, were never intended to remain
static. The multi-disciplinary team that authored the 1981 threshold study report outlined specific
triggers for standard review and set the expectation that the standards would be reassessed at least
every five years, writing, “environmental thresholds are not static standards that once in place remain
forever” (TRPA 1982a).
The presentation will provide an overview of the work underway to update threshold standards in two
focus areas.

STAFF REPORT

Date:       October 21, 2026

To:         TRPA Governing Board

From:       TRPA Staff

Subject:    Lake Tahoe Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) Program Update


Summary and Staff Recommendation:
TRPA staff will provide an update on the Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) program. The presentation will
cover all program areas including AIS prevention, control, monitoring, and rapid response for the past
year.

Lake Tahoe faces a constant and serious threat from the introduction and spread of aquatic invasive
species. AIS can harm native ecosystems, negatively impact recreation opportunities, and affect Lake
Tahoe’s famed water quality and clarity. The Lake Tahoe AIS program’s mission is to prevent, detect, and
control aquatic invasive species in the region so that future generations can enjoy Lake Tahoe.

TRPA co-leads the Lake Tahoe AIS program with the Tahoe Resource Conservation District (Tahoe RCD)
and more than 40 public and private partners. Numerous federal, state, and regional regulations and
programs are in place to limit the introduction and spread of AIS. TRPA and Tahoe RCD implement a
nationally recognized watercraft inspection program, work together to reduce and control the existing
invasive species in the lake, and conduct lake-wide monitoring to measure progress.

Staff will provide an overview of accomplishments, challenges, and upcoming work for the AIS program.
Staff will highlight program enhancements to protect the Tahoe Region from golden mussels and other
AIS. These enhancements include strategies focusing on motorized and non-motorized recreation,
education and outreach, as well as the status of permanent watercraft inspection stations.

Staff will also share progress on control activities including the next phase of work at the Taylor-Tallac
Ecosystem, Emerald Bay, and Nevada Shoreline areas, as well as interim control and containment work
at the Tahoe Keys and other locations around the lake.

Regarding monitoring, staff will discuss upcoming lake-wide surveys and surveillance, a new drone-
supported remote-sensing effort, and early detection monitoring.

Staff will close with the status of funding for the program and upcoming priorities.
This item is for informational purposes, and no action is required.

Date:       October 21, 2026

To:         TRPA Governing Board

From:       TRPA Staff

Subject:    September Financial Statements, Fiscal Year 2027 (FY 2027)


Summary and Staff Recommendation:
As of September 30, 2026, 3 months, or 25 percent of the fiscal year, were complete. Appropriations
from both states have been invoiced and received. Planning fees are on pace with the prior year and the
budget. Expenses are as expected, driven primarily by staff compensation and contracts. Staff
recommends acceptance of the September 2026 Financial Statements for FY 2027.

Required Motion:
In order to accept the September 2026 Financial Statements, the Board must make the following
motion, based on the staff report:

        1) A motion to accept the September 2026 Financial Statements

In order for motion to pass, an affirmative vote of any eight Board members is required.

Fiscal Year-to-Date Revenues and Expenses
Through September, the agency recognized $9.7 million in revenue, representing 27 percent of the
budget. Revenue was primarily driven by $8.0 million in state appropriations. $1.2 million in fee revenue
was recognized. Fee revenue was driven by Planning fees, which account for $0.6 million and are at 22
percent of the budget. $0.2 million in other rent revenue and interest income are on plan for the fiscal
year to date.

The agency incurred expenses of $3.5 million, representing 9 percent of the budget, through September.
$2.3 million of Compensation is on track at 21 percent of the budget. Contracts and other costs of $1.0
million are ramping as the Agency completes the first quarter of the work plan.

Through September the agency received $0.8 million in mitigation fees and made $0.1 million in
mitigation disbursements.

Date:       October 21, 2026

To:         TRPA Governing Board

From:       TRPA Staff

Subject:    Resolutions Amending the Application Fee Schedule, Mobility Mitigation Fee, & Rental
            Vehicle Mitigation Fee


Summary and Staff Recommendation:
Staff recommends that the Governing Board adopt the attached Resolution 2026-__ (Attachment A) to
adjust the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency (TRPA) filing fee schedule for inflation. This action will
increase the TRPA filing fee schedule by 3.2 percent and the Mobility Mitigation Fee by 3.2 percent. The
fee adjustments will take effect on Tuesday, January 19, 2027.

Additionally, staff recommends that the Governing Board adopt the attached Resolution 2026-__
(Attachment B) to adjust the TRPA Rental Vehicle Mitigation Fee (RVMF) for inflation. This action will
increase the Rental Vehicle Mitigation Fee to $6.53 per day. The adjustments will take effect on Friday,
January 1, 2027.

Required Motions:
In order to amend the fee schedule and the above-referenced mitigation fees, the Board must make the
following motions, based on the staff report:

        1) A motion to approve the attached Resolution 2026-__, as shown in Attachment A, and its
           Exhibit 1, amending the TRPA application filing fee schedule and Mobility Mitigation Fee.
        2) A motion to approve the attached Resolution 2026-__, as shown in Attachment B, amending
           the Rental Vehicle Mitigation Fee.

In order for each motion to pass, an affirmative vote of any eight Board members is required.

Proposed changes:
Planning Fees
TRPA proposes a 3.2 percent inflation adjustment to the filing fees outlined in Exhibit 1, Attachment A.
The TRPA Governing Board has approved filing fee schedule increases annually since 2018 pursuant to
its policy of adjusting the filing fee schedule based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The filing fee
increase is based on the Western Region CPI. The Western Region CPI is referenced by the Nevada
Revised Statutes (NRS) for inflation adjustments to local building permit fees. While TRPA is not required
to follow NRS for fee adjustments, it serves as guidance that is consistent with TRPA’s approach to fee
amendments.

Summary and Staff Recommendation:
Staff recommends that the Governing Board approve the proposed Settlement Agreement (Attachment
A), under which Brady Sessions (“Sessions”) agrees to pay $15,000 to TRPA within 30 days of Governing
Board approval of this Settlement Agreement for the unauthorized removal of two trees and addition of
coverage without a TRPA permit at the property located at 630 Grand Avenue, Placer County,
Assessor’s Parcel Number (APN) 085-142-021 (the “Sessions Property”).

Required Motions:
To approve the proposed Settlement Agreement, the Governing Board must make the following motion,
based on the staff report:

            A motion to approve the Settlement Agreement as shown in Attachment A.

For the motion to pass, an affirmative vote of any eight Board members is required.

Violation Description/Background:
In May 2026, TRPA investigated a report of unauthorized tree removal at the Sessions Property. After
further investigation, TRPA found that two large trees over 20 inches diameter at breast height (dbh)
had been removed for the construction of a new deck. Neither the tree removal activities nor deck
construction project sought or obtained a TRPA permit, resulting in several violations of the TRPA Code
of Ordinances (“Code”). The Code violations include the unauthorized creation of land coverage,
unauthorized grading activities without a pregrade inspection, disturbance of vegetation during
construction, and removal of trees greater than 14 inches dbh without TRPA approval.

Sessions has taken full responsibility for the unauthorized activities and has agreed to a settlement in
which he will pay a penalty of $15,000 to TRPA and either remove or obtain a permit for the deck

Summary and Staff Recommendation:
Staff recommends that the Governing Board approve the proposed Settlement Agreement (Attachment
A), under which LIND Art & Technology, Inc. (“LIND”) agrees to pay $10,000 to TRPA within 30 days of
Governing Board approval of this Settlement Agreement for use of motorized watercraft in violation of
the TRPA Code of Ordinances (“Code”), including use in the tributaries of Lake Tahoe and launching
without the required required aquatic invasive species (“AIS”) decontamination requirements.

Required Motions:
To approve the proposed Settlement Agreement, the Governing Board must make the following motion,
based on the staff report:

            A motion to approve the Settlement Agreement as shown in Attachment A.

For the motion to pass, an affirmative vote of any eight Board members is required.

Violation Description/Background:
LIND designs and sells electric surfboards and is operated through two affiliated entities: LIND Art &
Technology, Inc., a corporation based in San Francisco, California (“LIND”), and LIND Art & Technology
AB, a Swedish entity (“LIND AB”). LIND is the sole signatory to this Settlement Agreement, and all
references to “LIND” in this Agreement refer to LIND Art & Technology, Inc. unless otherwise specified.

In 2026, TRPA discovered social media content posted to official LIND social media channels that
depicted the use of LIND electric surfboards within Lake Tahoe and other waterbodies of the Lake Tahoe
basin. The electric surfboards manufactured by LIND are considered “motorized watercraft” under the
TRPA Code and are subject to Code provisions pertaining to motorized watercraft.

The content depicted (1) the launching of LIND electric surfboards into Lake Tahoe without required AIS
inspection and decontamination, (2) the use of LIND electric surfboards within Lake Tahoe in a manner
that created wakes within 600 feet of the waterline and within Emerald Bay, and (3) the use of LIND

This item is informational only.
Background:
More than forty years ago, the revised Bi-State Compact recognized that “the waters of Lake Tahoe and
other resources of the region are threatened with deterioration or degeneration, which endangers the
natural beauty and economic productivity of the region” (96th Congress, 1980). To protect these
resources for future generations, the Compact directs TRPA to establish “environmental threshold
carrying capacities,” defined as “an environmental standard necessary to maintain a significant scenic,
recreation, educational, scientific or natural value of the region or to maintain public health and safety
within the region.”
These standards set environmental quality goals and represent a shared aspiration to restore and
protect Lake Tahoe. The standards shape the goals and policies of the Regional Plan and guide millions
of dollars of public and private investment in the basin through the Environmental Improvement
Program (EIP).
The initial threshold standards, established more than four decades ago, were never intended to remain
static. The multi-disciplinary team that authored the 1981 threshold study report outlined specific
triggers for standard review and set the expectation that the standards would be reassessed at least
every five years, writing, “environmental thresholds are not static standards that once in place remain
forever” (TRPA 1982a).
The presentation will provide an overview of the work underway to update threshold standards in two
focus areas.

STAFF REPORT

Date:       October 21, 2026

To:         TRPA Governing Board

From:       TRPA Staff

Subject:    Lake Tahoe Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) Program Update


Summary and Staff Recommendation:
TRPA staff will provide an update on the Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) program. The presentation will
cover all program areas including AIS prevention, control, monitoring, and rapid response for the past
year.

Lake Tahoe faces a constant and serious threat from the introduction and spread of aquatic invasive
species. AIS can harm native ecosystems, negatively impact recreation opportunities, and affect Lake
Tahoe’s famed water quality and clarity. The Lake Tahoe AIS program’s mission is to prevent, detect, and
control aquatic invasive species in the region so that future generations can enjoy Lake Tahoe.

TRPA co-leads the Lake Tahoe AIS program with the Tahoe Resource Conservation District (Tahoe RCD)
and more than 40 public and private partners. Numerous federal, state, and regional regulations and
programs are in place to limit the introduction and spread of AIS. TRPA and Tahoe RCD implement a
nationally recognized watercraft inspection program, work together to reduce and control the existing
invasive species in the lake, and conduct lake-wide monitoring to measure progress.

Staff will provide an overview of accomplishments, challenges, and upcoming work for the AIS program.
Staff will highlight program enhancements to protect the Tahoe Region from golden mussels and other
AIS. These enhancements include strategies focusing on motorized and non-motorized recreation,
education and outreach, as well as the status of permanent watercraft inspection stations.

Staff will also share progress on control activities including the next phase of work at the Taylor-Tallac
Ecosystem, Emerald Bay, and Nevada Shoreline areas, as well as interim control and containment work
at the Tahoe Keys and other locations around the lake.

Regarding monitoring, staff will discuss upcoming lake-wide surveys and surveillance, a new drone-
supported remote-sensing effort, and early detection monitoring.

Staff will close with the status of funding for the program and upcoming priorities.
This item is for informational purposes, and no action is required.
